item.title: Deobfuscating Database Link Passwords in Oracle 26ai
item.description:
I recently encountered a scenario where I needed to deobfuscate the password of a database link user in Oracle 26ai. So, my plan was to quickly execute the db_link_password_decrypt_standalone.sql script written by Hatem Mahmoud (see also 1), but unfortunately, it failed with an error on Oracle 26ai.

item.title: Undocumented SYS_CONTEXT Parameters
item.description:
In Oracle, the SYS_CONTEXT function provides session and environment information to SQL and PL/SQL code. The function accepts a namespace, a parameter, and an optional length argument (see also 1):

Argument description:

  • namespace: a built-in or user-defined context namespace
  • parameter: the specific attribute to retrieve

item.title: Restricted and Undocumented oradebug Commands
item.description:
After an investigation into how to bypass restricted oradebug commands (see also 1), I started wondering whether a complete list of restricted commands exists, or whether there is any way to reliably identify them. Unfortunately, no such list is available, so I decided to take a closer look at the internal structures that oradebug uses under the hood.

To my surprise, I discovered that oradebug not only has restricted commands, but also a number of undocumented commands that are not shown in the oradebug help output.

item.title: SGA Changes in Oracle 26ai - Maximum Granule Size
item.description:
All memory components in the Oracle SGA are internally managed in fixed-size units called granules. They were introduced back in Oracle 9i as a standardized allocation unit that enables an Oracle instance to dynamically grow and shrink memory pools such as the buffer cache and shared pool at runtime in response to workload demands.

Memory for each pool is always allocated in whole granule units, and each pool requires at least one granule. Some memory pools can be subdivided into subpools and durations, and each of these smaller units requires a minimum of one granule. This means that a high number of subpools, and durations results in a higher memory footprint on a system. For a more detailed introduction and description of SGA granules, refer to sources 1, 2, and 3.

item.title: SGA Changes in Oracle 26ai - Subpools and Durations
item.description:
Oracle’s SGA memory management has undergone regular changes over the years and across different versions. Oracle 26ai is no exception and introduces another redesign of how SGA memory pools, such as the shared pool, are split into subpools and durations.

Historically, Oracle began splitting the shared pool into multiple subpools in version 9i and extended this approach in 10gR2 by further subdividing each of these subpools into smaller units called durations (you can also think of a duration as a “sub-subpool”).

item.title: Bypassing oradebug Restrictions
item.description:
In Oracle 26ai, the execution of certain oradebug commands and actions is no longer possible, as Oracle has changed the default value of the undocumented parameter _disable_oradebug_commands from none to restricted.

This change causes some oradebug functionality to stop working, as previously discussed by Jonathan Lewis in this blog post. Moreover, Mikhail Velikikh noted in a comment on the blog post that the parameter change from none to restricted was already introduced in RU 19.24.

item.title: UUID Generation In Oracle 26ai
item.description:
Some time ago, several bloggers wrote about the new support for UUIDs in Oracle 23ai/26ai (see the blog posts referenced in 1 and 2). This made me curious about how Oracle generates UUIDs behind the scenes and what exactly happens internally when a UUID is created. So, rather than discussing the pros and cons of UUIDs, this note provides a drill-down into Oracle’s UUID implementation details.

Oracle 23.7 introduced a new uuid() function, which generates 128-bit random UUIDv4 values compliant with RFC 9562. Historically, Oracle has provided the sys_guid() function, but the values it generates are predictable and not truly random.
